title: Quirks of the Mind · Episode 3
chapters: Why time flies, and why it drags

units.t: Quirks of the Mind. Episode three.
In this episode: When to trust your gut, Seeing patterns in random noise and Why time flies, and why it drags.
Part one. When to trust your gut.
Sometimes gut instinct beats careful analysis.
Sometimes it's dangerously wrong.
Here's how to tell the difference.
Two ways of thinking.
Daniel Kahneman, who won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics, popularised the idea of two systems in his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow.
System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless: recognising a face, sensing anger in a voice, knowing 2 plus 2.
System 2 is slow and deliberate: working out 17 times 24, parallel parking in a tight spot, or weighing a big decision.
Intuition is System 1 at work.
It handles most of daily life brilliantly, but it also produces predictable biases.
The two systems are a helpful metaphor, not two separate parts of the brain.
Intuition is recognition.
Psychologist Gary Klein studied firefighters making split-second decisions.
In one case, a commander ordered his crew out of a house moments before the floor collapsed, though he couldn't say why.
Later analysis suggested he'd noticed the fire was too quiet and the room too hot for a small kitchen fire: it was burning in the basement below.
Years of experience recognised the pattern faster than conscious thought.
Herbert Simon, another Nobel laureate, put it simply: intuition is nothing more and nothing less than recognition.

Kahneman and Klein, who began with opposite views, agreed in a 2009 paper on when to trust it: the environment must be regular enough to learn, and the person must have had lots of practice with quick, clear feedback.
Chess players, nurses, pilots and experienced tradies fit.
The key question is where the intuition was learned.
When it fails.
In some fields, experience doesn't build good intuition because outcomes are too random or feedback too delayed.
Stock pickers, political pundits and some long-range forecasters show little genuine skill, even though they feel confident.
Philip Tetlock's research on expert predictions, published in 2005, found many experts barely beat chance on long-term political forecasts, and often did worse than simple statistical rules.
Famous experts did no better than obscure ones.
Confidence comes from how coherent a story feels, not from how accurate it is.
Feeling certain and being correct can come apart.
Shortcuts and gut feelings.
In 1974, Amos Tversky and Kahneman described heuristics, the shortcuts intuition relies on.
The availability heuristic judges how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, which is why shark attacks and plane crashes feel likelier than they are.
With anchoring, an initial number pulls later estimates towards it, which is how an asking price shapes what a house seems worth.
Not every famous finding held up: some 'priming' studies Kahneman cited failed to replicate, and he acknowledged relying on them too heavily.
A feeling that someone is 'off' can reflect real cues, like inconsistent stories or pressure tactics, and shouldn't be dismissed when your safety is involved.
But gut reactions are also shaped by stereotypes and first impressions.
Unstructured job interviews feel insightful but predict performance less well than structured ones.
Training and using intuition.
Good intuition can be trained where feedback exists.
Write down predictions before you learn the outcome, then check them.
Tetlock's Good Judgment Project, run from 2011, found that ordinary volunteers who did this, updated their views often and thought in probabilities became strikingly accurate 'superforecasters'.
Keeping score turns vague hunches into measurable skill.
Notice your gut reaction, then ask whether you have real experience here with clear feedback.
If yes, give it weight.

If the decision is big, unfamiliar or emotionally charged, slow down: write out options, consider what would change your mind, and ask others, including a qualified professional for health, money or legal matters.
Kahneman suggested gathering the facts first, then forming your overall judgement.
Or make a guess, do the analysis, and compare.
Where they disagree, you've learned something.
The key idea: Psychologists describe fast intuitive thinking, System 1, and slow deliberate thinking, System 2, and intuition is System 1 at work.
Part two. Seeing patterns in random noise.
Shuffle a playlist and the same artist plays three times in a row.
Rigged?
Probably not.
Randomness is far lumpier than our brains expect.
Random looks clumpy.
Ask one group to invent 100 coin tosses and another to actually toss a coin 100 times.
Teachers who run this trick can usually spot the fakes.
Invented sequences switch between heads and tails too often and avoid long runs.
Real tosses often include a streak of five or six of the same result, because over 100 tosses such runs are quite likely.
Our intuition says random things should look evenly spread, like sprinkles on a cake.
In reality, randomness is clumpy.
Rain falls unevenly, stars cluster and buses arrive in bunches.
When we see a clump, our brains shout 'pattern', even when chance alone would produce it.
Bombs over London.
During the Second World War, German V-1 flying bombs fell on London.
Many residents were convinced the strikes were targeted, because some neighbourhoods were hit repeatedly while others were spared.
Rumours spread that German spies lived in the spared areas.
In 1946, a British actuary named R.
D.
Clarke divided a section of south London into hundreds of equal squares and counted the hits in each.
The counts closely matched what you would expect if the bombs had landed at random.
The clusters that felt so meaningful were just the natural clumping of chance.
This is now called the clustering illusion, and it still shapes how people read crime maps, disease outbreaks and accidents.
Painting the target.
Imagine a cowboy firing randomly at a barn.
Afterwards, he paints a bullseye around the tightest group of holes and declares himself a sharpshooter.
This joke names the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: finding a cluster first, then treating it as if it had been predicted.
It happens whenever people search lots of data, spot an interesting clump and forget how many other places they looked.
A town might seem to have an unusual number of a particular illness.
But there are thousands of towns and many kinds of illness, so somewhere, by chance, a striking cluster will appear.
Investigators take such reports seriously, and some turn out to be real.
Many, though, prove to be painted bullseyes.
Faces and shuffles.
In 1976, the Viking 1 spacecraft photographed a hill on Mars that looked startlingly like a human face.
Later, sharper images showed an ordinary eroded mesa.
Seeing meaningful images in random shapes, especially faces, is called pareidolia.
It probably reflects how vital it has been to recognise friends, enemies and emotions quickly.
The reverse also happens.
Users have complained that music shuffles weren't random because songs by one artist played close together.
Many apps now adjust shuffle so an artist doesn't repeat, because genuine randomness feels suspicious.
Likewise, many people feel that 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 could never win a lottery, though it is exactly as likely as any other combination.
Test before you trust.
Ask how many chances there were for a pattern to appear.
A one in a million coincidence is likely in a country of millions.
Decide what you are testing before you look, as scientists do by registering their plans in advance.
Then check whether the pattern holds in fresh data.
A real effect should reappear; a random clump usually won't.
Be humble in both directions.
For decades, researchers called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion.
In 2018, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo found a statistical bias in the original analysis and argued a modest effect may exist after all.
'It's just randomness' can be a mistake too.
The key idea: Real randomness contains streaks and clusters that feel deliberate.
Part three. Why time flies, and why it drags.
An hour in a dentist's waiting room crawls, while a week on holiday vanishes.
Yet looking back, the holiday feels longer.
Your sense of time is not a clock.
It is a story your brain tells.
No clock in the head.
We have eyes for light and ears for sound, but no dedicated sense organ for time.
The brain builds duration from many sources: neural rhythms, attention, emotion and how many new events we take in.
For intervals of a second or less, people are surprisingly precise.
For longer stretches, judgements are easily pushed around.
Psychologists distinguish between judging time as it passes, called prospective timing, and judging it afterwards, called retrospective timing.
While waiting for a kettle to boil, your attention keeps returning to time, and each check stretches the interval.
That is the grain of truth in 'a watched pot never boils'.
When absorbed, little attention is left for tracking time, and it flies.
Fear and anxiety can stretch time, while enjoyable focus shrinks it.
The holiday paradox.
A week of new sights on holiday seems to rush past, yet looking back it feels longer than a routine week at work.
The psychologist and broadcaster Claudia Hammond named this the holiday paradox.
The likely explanation is that, in hindsight, we judge durations partly by how many distinct memories we have from that period.
A holiday packed with novel experiences leaves many memories, so it seems long.
A routine week leaves few, and blurs into its neighbours.
The reverse happens with boredom: a dull afternoon drags while you live through it, then shrinks to almost nothing in memory.
Edited perception.
Many people describe crashes or falls as happening in slow motion.
In a 2007 study, the neuroscientist David Eagleman and colleagues had volunteers fall backwards from a tall tower into a safety net at a Texas amusement park.
They estimated their own fall lasted roughly a third longer than falls they watched.
But a wrist display flashed numbers too fast to read normally, and falling volunteers could not read them.
Frightening moments are not perceived in slow motion; they are remembered in rich detail, which makes them feel longer afterwards.
Chronostasis is a small cousin: after your eyes jump to an analogue clock, the second hand can seem to freeze for longer than a second, because the brain backdates what you see after the movement.
Why the years speed up.
A common complaint of adulthood is that the years rush by.
One popular explanation is that each year is a smaller fraction of your life, though this is hard to test.
A more research friendly idea links back to the holiday paradox: childhood and youth are full of firsts, while adult life often settles into routine, leaving fewer distinctive memories per year.
Surveys find that older people often say the last decade went quickly.
But studies asking about the past week or month show weaker age differences than you might expect.
The feeling seems to apply mostly to long stretches of time looked back upon.
Stretching your own time.
If remembered time depends on distinct memories, there are practical ways to make life feel fuller.
Breaking routines with small changes, such as a new walking route, a different weekend activity or learning a skill, gives memory more distinct markers to hold onto.
Travel, even locally, can do the same.
Paying deliberate attention, such as noticing details or recalling the day's events at the end of it, may also help experiences stick.
None of this makes the clock tick slower.
But since our sense of how long we have lived is built from memories rather than minutes, filling time with variety is the closest thing we have to stretching it.
The key idea: The brain has no organ for time, and paying attention to time passing makes it seem to slow.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is System 1 thinking?
Answer. Fast, automatic and intuitive.
Question two. How do invented 'random' coin sequences usually differ from real ones?
Answer. They switch sides too often.
Question three. Why does a kettle seem to take forever when you watch it?
Answer. Checking on time passing makes the interval seem longer.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
